subTopics.name: Using data to tell a story

dotPoints.description: Explain the purposes of data visualisation (simplifying understanding; telling a story; highlighting significant results)

prompts.question: Identify two main purposes of data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a business analyst at a retail company must present a quarter's sales figures to the executive team, who will have only a few minutes to grasp the results. The analyst has several thousand transaction records and must decide how to show the key results.
markerNotes: Name two distinct purposes in a few words each; an identify question does not need elaboration.
Syllabus-level purposes such as simplifying understanding, telling a story and highlighting significant results earn credit; 'to make data look nice' does not.
Two purposes that overlap, such as 'to show data' and 'to display data', count as one.
commonStudentErrors: Naming two chart types (e.g. bar chart and line chart) instead of two purposes of visualisation.
Writing 'to make the data look nice' as a purpose, without linking it to understanding or insight.
Restating one purpose in two wordings, such as 'to simplify data' and 'to make data easier to understand'.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct, correct purposes of data visualisation, such as simplifying understanding and telling a story, each stated clearly
1 mark: Identifies one correct purpose, or gives two purposes where one is vague or repeats the other

sampleAnswers.answer: Two main purposes of data visualisation are simplifying understanding, making complex datasets easy to grasp at a glance, and telling a story by highlighting significant results that lead the audience to a clear conclusion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both purposes are correct and distinct: simplifying understanding, and telling a story by highlighting significant results. Each is named clearly, so both marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: Data visualisation helps people understand data better. It also makes the data look more attractive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The first point is a correct purpose and earns one mark. 'Looks more attractive' is an aesthetic effect rather than a purpose, and the first point already covers understanding, so the second mark is not earned.

prompts.question: Explain how a well-designed data visualisation can be more effective at highlighting significant results than a raw table of data.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: an environmental scientist has recorded sea-level measurements from a coastal monitoring station over 20 years, producing several thousand rows of readings. The scientist must brief a council's policy team on the rising trend and is deciding whether to present a chart or the raw table.
markerNotes: Name the visual mechanism (position, slope, colour or contrast) and say what it does for the reader; 'it looks better' earns no credit.
Compare directly with the table: a chart shows a trend or outlier at a glance, while a table requires searching and mental comparison.
Use the sea-level example to ground the explanation, such as a steep line rising at the end of the record.
commonStudentErrors: Describing chart features (title, legend, axes) without explaining how any feature highlights a result.
Calling a graph 'better' or 'more professional' than a table without stating why it makes significant results easier to find.
Writing about the sea-level data in general (sea levels are rising) rather than about how the visualisation shows the significant result.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Clearly explains how specific visual features of a well-designed visualisation (such as position, length, colour or contrast) direct attention to significant results, and contrasts this with the effort needed to find the same result in a raw table, using an example from the sea-level data
3 marks: Explains how a well-designed visualisation highlights significant results using a relevant visual feature and a comparison with a raw table, but the explanation or example is underdeveloped
2 marks: States that a visualisation makes results easier to see than a table, with a general reason such as 'the trend is easier to see', but does not explain which visual features do this
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported statement about visualisations, such as 'charts are more interesting than tables', with no link to highlighting significant results

sampleAnswers.answer: A well-designed data visualisation is more effective at highlighting significant results because it uses visual contrast to direct attention to what matters. In a sea-level chart, a steeply rising line drawn in a contrasting colour makes the long-term increase visible at a glance. A raw table of several thousand readings forces the reader to search and compare numbers before any trend can be seen. The visualisation therefore does the work of simplifying understanding, while the table leaves that work to the audience. Pre-attentive features such as slope and colour let the reader spot trends and outliers in seconds, so the key message reaches the policy team quickly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: specific visual features are named (a steeply rising line, a contrasting colour), the sea-level example grounds the point, and the chart is contrasted with the raw table. The explanation of how visual contrast lets the reader spot trends and outliers in seconds is what separates explanation from description.

sampleAnswers.answer: A chart is better than a table because it is easier to read. For example, a line graph of sea levels shows the sea going up over time, so people can see the trend quickly. A table would have all the numbers and people would have to read through them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant point and an example are given, which earns two marks. The answer does not name the visual feature doing the work or explain how it draws the eye to the significant result. Name the feature, such as a steeply rising line, and explain its effect to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Data visualisations are colourful and look professional, which makes sea level data more interesting. Tables are boring to read.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The statement is relevant to the question but unsupported: 'looks professional' and 'more interesting' are opinions with no link to highlighting significant results. Explain what the visual shows that the table does not.

dotPoints.description: Describe how features of software contribute to a better understanding of datasets through data visualisation, including spreadsheets, creative design applications and combining applications to track trends and forecast

prompts.question: Identify two features of spreadsheet software that can be used to create data visualisations.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a Year 11 student has a table of weekly sales from a school cafe in a spreadsheet and needs to turn it into a chart for a class presentation.
markerNotes: Name the feature itself, such as 'charting tools' or 'conditional formatting'; a general word such as 'graphs' is weaker.
Each feature must relate to creating or supporting visualisations, not to general file management such as saving or printing.
Two features are needed: one feature described two ways earns one mark.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a file action such as saving or printing as a visualisation feature.
Giving one feature twice in different words, such as 'charts' and 'graphs'.
Naming a chart type, such as a pie chart, as a feature rather than the tool that creates it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct spreadsheet features that create or support visualisations, such as built-in charting tools and conditional formatting, each named clearly
1 mark: Identifies one correct spreadsheet feature that creates or supports visualisations, or names two features where one is not relevant to visualisation, such as saving files

sampleAnswers.answer: Spreadsheet software offers two features for data visualisation: built-in charting tools, which turn selected cells into bar, line or pie charts, and conditional formatting, which colours cells according to their values.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two distinct visualisation features, charting tools and conditional formatting, are named and briefly described. Both marks are earned because each is a feature used to present data visually.

sampleAnswers.answer: A spreadsheet can make a chart from a selected table of data. Spreadsheets also let you save the file, which is useful for sharing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Creating a chart from selected data is a correct feature and earns one mark. Saving the file is not a visualisation feature, so it earns nothing. Replace it with a second feature such as conditional formatting or colour scales.

prompts.question: Describe how an analyst could combine a spreadsheet application with a creative design application to produce a high-quality infographic.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a marketing team at a small clothing retailer wants an infographic summarising the age groups and locations of its online customers for a board presentation. The customer records are in a spreadsheet, and the team has a creative design application available.
markerNotes: Show the sequence: data processing in the spreadsheet, then export of charts or figures, then layout and styling in the design application.
Explain each tool's role at its stage: the spreadsheet for calculation and charting, the design tool for layout, typography and visual narrative.
Anchor the description in the marketing scenario, such as choosing the demographic breakdowns that matter to the team.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the design application alone, with no account of how the spreadsheet prepares the data.
Saying the spreadsheet 'makes the infographic' without describing the steps taken to move between the two tools.
Listing features of each program, such as templates, without saying how the work passes from one to the other.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes a clear, sequenced workflow in which the spreadsheet is used to clean, summarise and chart the customer data, the outputs are exported to a creative design application, and the design tool is used to build a layout, brand-consistent styling and a narrative. Explains why each tool suits its stage
3 marks: Describes both tools and a sensible sequence, with one stage underdeveloped or without an explanation of what the design application adds
2 marks: Describes the spreadsheet's role in some detail, or both tools' roles in general terms, without showing how the two combine
1 mark: Makes a relevant but general statement about the tools, such as 'the spreadsheet holds the data and the design tool makes it look good', with no description of how they are combined

sampleAnswers.answer: An analyst would first use the spreadsheet application to process the raw customer records. A pivot table summarises customer demographics such as age group and location, and basic charts reveal the key patterns in the data. The analyst would then export those charts and figures into a creative design application such as Adobe Illustrator or Canva. There, the data visualisation is no longer limited by the spreadsheet's formatting: charts are placed into a custom layout, brand colours and icons are applied, and short text supports the storytelling. The result is a polished infographic that presents a clear story to the board.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer sets out the sequence from spreadsheet analysis to design layout and explains what each tool contributes. It stays with the marketing scenario, so the workflow is one the team could follow.

sampleAnswers.answer: The analyst could use a spreadsheet's pivot tables to summarise the customer ages and locations, then create a bar chart from the results. The chart could then be placed into a design program.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The spreadsheet's role is described in detail, but the design application is only mentioned and not described. Explain what the design tool contributes to the infographic, such as layout, colour and text, to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A spreadsheet holds the customer data and a design program makes the final infographic look nice. The two are combined by copying the data into the design program.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer names each tool's broad purpose, which is relevant but general. 'Copying the data' is not an accurate account of how the tools combine. Describe the specific steps: what is charted, how it is exported and how the layout is built.

dotPoints.description: Identify patterns in data by interpreting and comparing datasets for an enterprise, social or ethical issue to highlight trends and for predictive data analytics

prompts.question: Distinguish between a pattern and a trend in data analytics.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: an analyst at a regional bakery is reviewing five years of monthly sales records to decide how many staff to roster in each season.
markerNotes: Define each term separately, then state the difference: a trend has a direction over time, while a pattern repeats in a regular way.
A concrete example from the bakery data, such as a steady rise in annual sales (trend) or a December peak (pattern), makes the distinction clear.
commonStudentErrors: Treating a trend and a pattern as the same thing, with no distinction between direction over time and repetition.
Defining a pattern as 'something noticeable in the data' without saying that it repeats or follows a regularity.
Giving a one-off spike or outlier as an example of a pattern.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Distinguishes the two terms correctly: a trend is the long-term direction of change in the data, while a pattern is a recurring regularity that repeats, such as a seasonal peak, with an example for at least one
1 mark: Gives one accurate definition, such as 'a trend is the general direction data moves over time', or defines both terms too vaguely to separate them

sampleAnswers.answer: A trend is the long-term direction data moves in, such as a bakery's sales rising steadily each year. A pattern is a recurring regularity, such as a December sales peak. Both feed predictive data analytics using historical data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both terms are defined correctly and the difference is stated: a trend is the long-term direction and a pattern is a recurring regularity. The bakery sales examples confirm each definition, so both marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: A trend is when the data goes up or down over time. A pattern is when things in the data are noticed by the analyst.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The trend definition is correct and earns one mark. The pattern definition is too vague to count because it does not say that the pattern repeats. Define a pattern as a recurring regularity and give a bakery example.

prompts.question: A city council is comparing datasets on public transport usage and air quality levels over the past five years. Explain how identifying a pattern or trend in this data could be used for predictive data analytics.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a city council is comparing five years of monthly public transport patronage figures with air quality readings from monitoring stations in the same city. The council wants to know whether the data can support forecasts to inform its environmental policy.
markerNotes: Name a pattern or trend the council could find in the two datasets, then explain the step from that finding to a forecast.
Predictive analytics uses historical relationships to estimate future values; stating the assumption that past relationships will continue strengthens the explanation.
A correlation does not prove causation; noting this shows a more careful explanation.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the two datasets separately without identifying any pattern or trend that connects them.
Claiming the data will 'predict the future' without explaining how a model would use the historical relationship.
Describing what happened in the past five years, which is descriptive rather than predictive analytics.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how identifying a specific pattern or trend across the two datasets (such as a relationship between transport use and pollution, or a recurring seasonal cycle) provides a basis for predictive analytics, showing how historical relationships are used to build a model or forecast and how the council could act on it, with each step clearly linked
3 marks: Explains how an identified trend or pattern is used to forecast future values, with a relevant link to the transport and air quality data, but the mechanism or the link to policy is underdeveloped
2 marks: Identifies a pattern or trend in the data and states that it could be used to predict the future, without explaining how the prediction would be made
1 mark: Makes a general statement that data can predict the future, with no reference to the datasets or to a pattern identified in them

sampleAnswers.answer: Overlaying the two datasets, the council could identify a pattern: over five years, months with higher public transport patronage tend to coincide with lower pollution readings. This trend is the basis for predictive data analytics. Using the historical records, the council could build a model that forecasts how air quality would respond to a new bus route. The model assumes past relationships will continue, so its forecasts are only as reliable as the data behind them. Because correlation does not prove causation, the council should test the forecasts before using them to guide environmental policy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: a specific pattern and trend across the two datasets are identified, the forecasting step is explained, and the assumption behind the model is stated. The answer also notes that correlation does not prove causation and links the forecasts to policy.

sampleAnswers.answer: The council could look at the two datasets together and spot a pattern, such as air quality being better in months when public transport use is higher. This could be used to predict future air quality, because the council would know what the pattern is.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A pattern is identified and linked to a prediction, which earns two marks. The answer does not explain how historical data would be turned into a forecast, such as by building a model. Explain the modelling step to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Predictive analytics is when data is used to predict things. Councils use data to make decisions, so this could help them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The statement is accurate in general terms but does not refer to the transport or air quality data or to any pattern in it. Name a specific pattern in the two datasets and show how it leads to a forecast.

dotPoints.description: Investigate the impact of the evolution of hardware and software on the field of data analytics (processing power; storage/memory; communication media)

prompts.question: Outline how the evolution of processing power (CPU/GPU) has impacted data analytics.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a data analytics team is writing a short history section for an internal report on how its analysis tools have changed over the past twenty years.
markerNotes: An outline is a brief sketch of the main points: two impacts, each stated in a sentence, is the target.
Link each development (multi-core CPUs, GPUs) to an effect on analytics, such as faster queries or practical machine learning.
Naming the hardware is not enough; state what analysts can now do that they could not do before.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a history of computer hardware, such as early mainframes, instead of the impact on analytics.
Naming CPUs and GPUs as the impact itself, without stating what changed for analysts.
Claiming faster processors make data cleaning or quality checks unnecessary.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Outlines two distinct impacts of improved processing power on data analytics, such as faster processing and querying of large datasets with multi-core CPUs, and the practical use of computationally intensive machine learning, which GPUs support through parallel processing
1 mark: Outlines one correct impact of improved processing power on analytics, or names CPU and GPU developments without linking them to analytics

sampleAnswers.answer: Greater processing power from multi-core CPUs and GPUs has improved data analytics by letting analysts query large datasets faster. It also makes computationally intensive machine learning practical, because GPUs run many calculations in parallel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two distinct impacts are outlined: faster processing and querying of large datasets, and practical machine learning. Each is linked to what analysts can now do, which is what an outline must show.

sampleAnswers.answer: Computers today are much faster than they used to be, which is why analysts use GPUs. This means that analysis is quicker.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer names the hardware and one general speed benefit, which earns one mark. It does not identify a specific change for analytics, such as handling larger datasets or running machine learning, and the 'which is why' link is unsupported.

prompts.question: Investigate how advancements in BOTH storage/memory and communication media have enabled modern cloud-based data analytics.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional logistics company stores several years of delivery and vehicle sensor data in a cloud service such as Google BigQuery or Amazon S3. Its analysts work from several offices and query the same data each week.
markerNotes: The stem asks for both storage/memory and communication media; an answer that covers one area only cannot reach the middle bands.
Show the link: cheap storage made large datasets practical to keep, and fast networks made it practical to move them to the cloud for analysis.
Use the logistics scenario to show a concrete consequence, such as analysts in several offices querying the same warehouse.
commonStudentErrors: Covering only storage, or only networks, although the question asks for both.
Listing specifications such as 'SSDs are fast' without saying how they enabled cloud analytics.
Treating storage (keeping data) and memory (RAM used during processing) as the same thing.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Investigates how advances in storage and memory (such as cheap, high-capacity cloud storage, solid-state drives and larger RAM) and in communication media (such as high-bandwidth fibre networks) each enabled cloud analytics, and explains how they work together so large datasets can be stored, moved and processed, applied to the logistics scenario
3 marks: Explains how advances in both storage or memory and communication media enabled cloud analytics, with a clear link between them, but one area is developed in less depth or is not applied to the scenario
2 marks: Describes one advance, in storage or memory or in communication media, and how it enabled cloud analytics, with the other area only mentioned
1 mark: Makes a general statement that technology has improved analytics, with no specific advance in storage, memory or communication media named

sampleAnswers.answer: Advances in storage and memory have made cloud-based data analytics economically feasible. Cheap, high-capacity cloud storage, together with solid-state drives in data centres, lets enterprises keep big data sets and historical records on hand, while larger RAM allows analytics engines to hold working datasets in memory for rapid querying. Advances in communication media have made these remote resources practical to use. High-bandwidth fibre networks allow the logistics company's sensor and delivery data to reach a data warehouse in the cloud and be queried by analysts in several offices. Without this bandwidth, cheap storage would be negated by slow transfers, so the two advances work together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: both areas are investigated with specific advances, and the answer explains how they work together. The scenario is used to show the consequence for analysts across several offices, and the cloud-based analytics link is explicit.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cheap cloud object storage means a logistics company can keep several years of delivery records in one place and analyse them without buying its own servers. Better internet connections also help with cloud analytics.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The storage advance is explained with a clear consequence, which earns two marks. Communication media is only mentioned as 'better internet connections', with no account of what changed or how it enabled analytics. Investigate the specific network advance to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Modern computers have better storage and faster internet, which makes data analytics better in the cloud. Cloud services like Google BigQuery are popular for businesses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general statement that technology has improved analytics, so one mark. It does not name a specific advance or explain how it enabled cloud analytics. Name one advance in each area and explain its effect.

dotPoints.description: Describe online analytical processing (OLAP)

prompts.question: State the primary function of an OLAP system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a retail chain's business manager wants to explore three years of sales data by product, region and month, changing the view on screen without waiting for a new report.
markerNotes: The primary function is fast, interactive, multidimensional analysis, as distinct from recording individual transactions, which is the role of OLTP systems.
A short answer suits STATE, but it must include the multidimensional element; 'it analyses data' is too general.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that OLAP records or stores transactions, which describes transaction processing rather than analysis.
Writing 'OLAP is for analysis' without saying what kind of analysis, such as multidimensional or interactive.
Confusing OLAP with a chart type or a spreadsheet, rather than a system for querying data.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: States the primary function of OLAP accurately: enabling fast, interactive, multidimensional analysis of large volumes of data, typically held in a data warehouse, such as viewing sales by product, time and location
1 mark: States a partial function, such as 'it analyses data', without the multidimensional or interactive element

sampleAnswers.answer: The primary function of OLAP, or online analytical processing, is to allow fast, interactive, multidimensional analysis of large sales data, such as viewing sales by product, region and month, typically held in a data warehouse.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The function is stated accurately with its key elements: fast, interactive, multidimensional analysis of large volumes of data, typically held in a data warehouse. The multidimensional element is what earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: An OLAP system is used to analyse data, which helps managers make decisions about their business.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The statement is correct but general, so it earns one mark. It does not identify the interactive, multidimensional character of OLAP, which is what distinguishes it from other analysis. Add that users can view the data from several dimensions, such as product, time and location.

prompts.question: Describe how an OLAP cube would allow a retail manager to analyse sales data. Use the dimensions of 'Product', 'Time', and 'Location' in your answer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a national retail chain's regional manager needs to understand sales performance in detail. The sales data is organised by product, time and store location, and the manager wants answers without writing database queries.
markerNotes: Define each operation in one clause, then give an example using the named dimensions, such as slicing on Product or drilling from year to quarter on Time.
Describe the cube as storing pre-calculated summaries across its dimensions, and say why this makes responses quick for the manager.
Use the three named dimensions throughout; an answer that omits one of them loses the 'use the dimensions' requirement.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the cube as a 3D chart or graphic, rather than a data structure for multidimensional analysis.
Confusing slice and dice, for example by describing a dice as selecting one product.
Describing drill down as zooming in on a chart, rather than moving to a lower level of a dimension such as from year to month.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes how the cube's Product, Time and Location dimensions let the manager navigate sales measures, explaining slice (one value of one dimension), dice (a sub-cube across two or more dimensions) and drill down (moving from a summary to finer detail on a dimension such as Time), each with a concrete example from the retail scenario
3 marks: Describes the cube's dimensions and at least two operations, such as slice and drill down, with an example of one, but one operation or example is underdeveloped or unclear
2 marks: Describes the cube as organising sales by Product, Time and Location, and gives one way the manager could analyse it, with limited detail
1 mark: States that an OLAP cube is a multidimensional structure or stores sales data, without showing how the manager would use the dimensions

sampleAnswers.answer: An OLAP cube would pre-calculate and store sales data across the dimensions of Product, Time, and Location. This allows the retail manager to perform multi-dimensional analysis with near-instantaneous results. For example, they could 'slice' the cube to view total sales for a single 'Product' across all times and locations. They could 'dice' the cube to look at a very specific intersection, like sales of 'Laptops' in 'Sydney' during 'December'. They could also 'drill down' on the 'Time' dimension to move from viewing total annual sales to breaking it down by quarter, month, and then day, all without writing complex database queries.
sampleAnswers.feedback: All three named dimensions are used, and each operation is defined and illustrated with a retail example. The move from annual to monthly and daily Time detail shows how the manager explores the data.

sampleAnswers.answer: An OLAP cube organises sales by Product, Time and Location, so the manager can look at the sales data in different ways. For example, they could look at the sales for one product across all locations.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The cube and its dimensions are described, and one way of using it is given, which earns two marks. The operation is not named or explained. Name slice, dice and drill down and explain how each works on the Time dimension to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: An OLAP cube is a special type of database that stores sales data. It is useful because it is faster than other databases.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer correctly says the cube stores data, but it does not mention the dimensions or show how the manager would analyse the data. The speed claim is unsupported in this context. Describe how the manager would use Product, Time and Location.

dotPoints.description: Assess data integrity in the development of a data visualisation (ownership; source; validation; risk)

prompts.question: Distinguish between a data source and data validation in the context of data integrity.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a small team is preparing a dataset of school attendance figures, supplied as a spreadsheet by a school, for a public dashboard. Before the dashboard goes live, the team must confirm that the data can be trusted.
markerNotes: Define the source as origin and ownership, and validation as a checking process applied to the data, then state the difference.
Validation is an activity performed on the data, while the source is a fact about where it came from; the contrast is what earns the second mark.
Linking both terms to integrity, meaning accuracy and trustworthiness, strengthens the answer without adding length.
commonStudentErrors: Defining data validation as 'where the data came from' or as 'who owns the data'.
Treating source and validation as synonyms, both meaning 'checking the data'.
Describing data integrity as 'having a lot of data' rather than the accuracy and trustworthiness of the data.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Distinguishes the two terms clearly: a data source is where the data came from, including who collected or owns it, while data validation is the process of checking the data's accuracy, completeness and consistency before it is used
1 mark: Defines one term correctly, or describes both in general terms that do not show how they differ

sampleAnswers.answer: A data source is where the data comes from, including its ownership. Data validation is the process of checking the accuracy and completeness of the data before a data visualisation is built, protecting data integrity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The source is defined as origin and validation as a checking process, with the difference stated clearly. Both are linked to integrity through accuracy and completeness, which is what the question tests.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data source is a place where data comes from, such as a spreadsheet or a website. Data validation is also about the data and helps make sure it is good.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The source is defined correctly, which earns one mark. The validation definition is too vague: 'makes sure it is good' does not say what is checked. Name the checks, such as accuracy, completeness and consistency, to earn the second mark.

prompts.question: Assess the risk to an enterprise that creates a public-facing data visualisation based on data from an unverified third-party source.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a consumer goods company downloads a dataset from an unfamiliar website showing rapid growth in its product category, and places a chart based on it on its public website and in marketing materials. Nobody on the team has checked who produced the dataset or how it was collected.
markerNotes: Assess means judge the size of the risk: link the unverified source to the visualisation's integrity, then to consequences for the company, then judge how serious it is.
Name the consequence, such as customers relying on wrong figures, reputational damage, or a complaint about copyright or terms of use, rather than saying 'bad things could happen'.
A reasoned judgement, such as 'the risk is high because errors cannot be corrected once the chart is published', is needed for the upper bands.
commonStudentErrors: Listing risks without judging how serious they are, which describes rather than assesses.
Assuming the data is wrong because it came from the internet, rather than saying its accuracy is unknown because it is unverified.
Writing only about the cost of the campaign, not about public and reputational consequences.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Assesses the risk with reasoned judgement: explains that the unverified source leaves the visualisation's accuracy unknown, that publishing it exposes the company to reputational damage and loss of trust, and that decisions or legal exposure could follow, then judges how serious the overall risk is
3 marks: Identifies and explains the main risks to integrity and to the company's reputation, with a judgement of their seriousness, but one risk or the judgement is underdeveloped
2 marks: Identifies one or two relevant risks, such as inaccurate data or reputational damage, with limited explanation and no clear judgement
1 mark: States a risk in general terms, such as 'the visualisation could be wrong', without explaining its consequences for the company

sampleAnswers.answer: The overall risk to the enterprise is high. Because the third-party source is unverified, the data integrity of the data visualisation is unknown, and the figures may be inaccurate, biased or outdated. Without data validation, no one can show that the chart is accurate, and the unknown ownership of the dataset means its copyright status is also unclear. Publishing the chart risks misleading customers, causing reputational damage and a loss of trust. Decisions based on it could also lead to financial losses. The risk is high because a published error spreads quickly and cannot be recalled from every audience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer assesses rather than lists: it links the unknown integrity to reputational and decision-making consequences, and judges the risk as high with a reason. The copyright point is hedged, which suits an unverified dataset.

sampleAnswers.answer: Using unverified data could mean the chart is wrong, and customers may stop trusting the company. This could hurt the business.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two relevant risks, inaccuracy and loss of trust, are identified, which earns two marks. The answer does not explain why an unverified source makes the data unreliable or judge how serious the risk is. Add both to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: There is a risk because the data came from the internet.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A risk is named but not explained or linked to consequences for the company, so one mark. Explain what happens if the data is wrong, such as misleading customers, and how serious that would be.

dotPoints.description: Explain the impact of enterprise data warehousing on data visualisation (analysis and use of historical data trends and patterns; correlation with current data; data refinement/optimisation)

prompts.question: Outline one major benefit a data warehouse provides for data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a mid-sized enterprise wants one dashboard showing data from its sales, marketing and human resources systems. The three systems store their records separately and in different formats.
markerNotes: One benefit, developed in two sentences, is the target: name it, then explain how it improves the visualisation.
'Single source of truth' is a recognised benefit, but explain what it means: consistent, integrated data from sales, marketing and HR systems.
Storing data is not a benefit in itself; the benefit lies in the integration, cleaning and consistency the warehouse provides.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the data warehouse 'stores data' without saying how this helps the visualisation.
Naming a benefit such as faster charts without explaining why the warehouse causes it.
Confusing a data warehouse with an ordinary operational database used for transactions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Outlines one major benefit of a data warehouse for visualisation, such as a single integrated source of clean, consistent data from several systems, and briefly explains why this matters for the dashboard
1 mark: Names a benefit in general terms, such as 'it stores data', or names a benefit without explaining its effect on visualisation

sampleAnswers.answer: Enterprise data warehousing integrates sales, marketing and HR records into one consistent data warehouse, including historical data. This single source of truth lets a dashboard give data visualisation that agrees across all three systems.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One major benefit is named and explained in terms of its effect on the visualisation: records from several systems are integrated into one consistent warehouse, so the dashboard shows data that agrees. Both marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data warehouse stores a lot of data in one place, which is useful for an enterprise.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Storage is named, but the answer does not show how it helps the visualisation, and storing a lot of data is not the warehouse's main benefit. Explain that integrating data from several systems gives the dashboard one consistent dataset.

prompts.question: Explain how a data warehouse enables an enterprise to create visualisations that correlate historical data trends with current data.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a retail company wants a dashboard that compares this month's sales with the same month in each of the previous ten years, so managers can tell whether a recent rise is unusual. Its transaction records are held in an operational system designed for day-to-day processing.
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism: warehouses store integrated, time-stamped data over long periods, so one query can cover the last ten years and the current month.
Link the comparison to a decision, such as whether this month's sales are unusually high or part of a recurring seasonal pattern.
Contrast the operational system (current, transaction-focused) with the warehouse (history, analysis-focused) to show why the warehouse is used.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the warehouse 'shows the data on a graph' without explaining how historical and current data are brought together.
Describing historical data only, without showing how current data enters the visualisation.
Treating the warehouse as a visualisation tool, rather than a store of integrated data that visualisation tools connect to.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how a data warehouse, which stores integrated, time-stamped historical data separately from day-to-day operational systems, lets analysts query past and current data together, so that a visualisation can place current figures alongside long-term trends, and explains what this lets managers judge, such as whether this month is unusual or seasonal
3 marks: Explains that the warehouse holds historical data alongside current data and that a visualisation can compare them, with a clear example, but the reason the warehouse makes this possible is underdeveloped
2 marks: Identifies that a data warehouse stores historical data and that a visualisation can show it alongside current figures, without explaining how the comparison is made possible or what it shows
1 mark: States a general benefit of data warehouses, such as storing lots of data, with no link to historical trends or to current data in visualisations

sampleAnswers.answer:
Enterprise data warehousing stores integrated, time-stamped records separately from the operational system. A data warehouse therefore keeps historical data over many years, so one query can cover ten years of sales alongside the current month. The operational system is designed for current transactions and may overwrite records, whereas the warehouse preserves snapshots of past sales.

A data visualisation tool can query the warehouse for the same month in each previous year and plot current data against those trends. The dashboard shows the correlation between this month's sales and the historical range, letting managers see whether a rise sits within the normal seasonal pattern or outside it, and whether it is a genuine change or a recurring cycle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the warehouse's integrated, time-stamped storage is explained, the contrast with the operational system is drawn, and the correlation of current data with historical trends is tied to a managerial judgement about whether a rise is unusual.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data warehouse stores historical sales, so a dashboard can show sales from previous years. The dashboard can also show this month's sales next to those figures, so managers can compare them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The historical storage and the comparison with current sales are both identified, which earns two marks. The answer does not explain how the warehouse makes the comparison reliable or what managers can judge from it. Explain the integrated, time-stamped storage to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data warehouse is a large storage system that can hold a lot of data. Dashboards can then be made with the data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general description of storage, so one mark. There is no reference to historical trends, current data or how the visualisation correlates them. Name the historical element and explain how it is compared with current figures.

dotPoints.description: Explain how big data affects the design and development of data visualisation (scope of visible information; types and depth of insight provided by the data)

prompts.question: Identify two design challenges that big data creates for data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a designer is building a map of national bus journeys from a transport dataset that records billions of GPS points over a year. The designer must decide what the chart will show and how it will load.
markerNotes: Name the challenge and its effect on the design: overplotting hides patterns, and slow rendering prevents interaction.
The two challenges should differ: visual clutter is a design problem and performance is a technical one.
A challenge is a problem for the designer, not a benefit of big data; 'big data gives more information' earns no credit here.
commonStudentErrors: Stating a benefit of big data, such as more insight, rather than a challenge for the designer.
Giving two wordings of the same problem, such as 'too many points' and 'the chart is cluttered'.
Naming general data problems such as bad data without linking them to big data.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct design challenges created by big data, such as visual clutter from very many data points and the performance demands of rendering large datasets, each named clearly
1 mark: Identifies one correct challenge, or names two points that describe the same problem in different words

sampleAnswers.answer: Two design challenges big data creates for data visualisation are visual clutter, where millions of data points hide patterns and limit the scope of visible information, and rendering performance, as large datasets load slowly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two distinct challenges are named: visual clutter from millions of data points, which is a design problem, and rendering performance, which is technical. Each is linked to a consequence, so both marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: Big data is hard to show in a chart because there is so much of it. The chart might also be hard to read because it has too much in it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both points describe the same problem, too much data on the chart, so the answer earns one mark. Name a different challenge, such as slow rendering of millions of points.

prompts.question: Explain how visualising 'big data' can provide deeper and different types of insight compared to visualising a small dataset. Use an example in your answer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a national retailer can visualise either a survey of 200 customers or every transaction its stores recorded over three years. Managers want to know which visualisation would reveal more about their customers.
markerNotes: The stem asks for different types of insight as well as deeper insight: say what kind (such as segment-level patterns or rare events) and why only large data reveals it.
Use an example that a small dataset could not show, such as a rare product fault in one region, to make the difference concrete.
Explain the mechanism: a sample of 200 may miss a subgroup or a rare event, while the full transaction record contains enough cases to show it.
commonStudentErrors: Saying big data is simply 'more accurate' without describing the different insight it provides.
Giving an example that would work equally well for a small dataset, so it does not show what scale adds.
Writing only about data storage or collection, without the visualisation side of the question.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains that visualising big data reveals different kinds of insight, not just more precise versions of the same ones: granular, segment-level patterns and rare events that a small sample hides, using a specific example that compares the two datasets
3 marks: Explains that big data reveals more detailed or different patterns than a small dataset, with a relevant example, but the reason for the difference (scale, granularity or sampling) is underdeveloped
2 marks: States that big data gives deeper insight than a small dataset, with a general example, without explaining what kind of insight is gained
1 mark: Makes a general claim that more data is better, with no reference to the type of insight or to visualisation

sampleAnswers.answer:
Visualising big data can reveal different types of insight that are impossible to detect in a small dataset. While a small sample might show only an average trend, a big data visualisation exposes variation and outliers with much higher confidence.

For example, visualising a survey of 200 customers might suggest that 'Product A' is popular. Visualising every transaction recorded over three years, however, can reveal a deeper insight: 'Product A' is extremely popular, but only with customers aged 18-24 in metropolitan areas. This segment-level pattern is visible only because the big data set contains enough cases in each segment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer goes beyond 'more data is better' by naming a different type of insight, a segment-level pattern that a survey of 200 customers cannot show, and comparing it directly with the small dataset. The example is specific enough to show what scale adds.

sampleAnswers.answer: Big data gives more information, so visualising it shows deeper insights than a small dataset. For example, a company with millions of sales records can see more about its customers than a company with a small survey.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Deeper insight is claimed and a general example is given, which earns two marks. The answer does not say what kind of insight is gained or why scale produces it. Describe one pattern that only the large dataset would reveal to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Big data is good because there is more of it. Visualisations are useful and help people look at data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general claim that more data is better, with no reference to the type of insight visualising it provides, so one mark. Name a specific insight, such as a pattern within a customer segment, and explain why the small dataset could not show it.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate bias in data collection, storage and analysis when developing visualisations (accuracy; audience; data source; unconscious bias)

prompts.question: Distinguish between bias from a data source and audience bias in the context of a data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a news website publishes a bar chart of how residents feel about a proposed development. The chart is based on an online poll that only visitors to the website could take, and readers bring their own views to the chart.
markerNotes: Locate each bias: data source bias sits in how the data was collected, while audience bias sits in the viewer's interpretation.
A concrete example, such as an online-only poll that misses people without internet access, shows the difference clearly.
Naming confirmation bias as an example of audience bias shows understanding of how viewers interpret charts.
commonStudentErrors: Defining audience bias as the audience being 'biased' in general, with no link to how they interpret the chart.
Attributing data source bias to the chart's colours or layout, which belong to the design rather than the data.
Describing both biases as the same thing, such as 'the chart is unfair'.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Distinguishes the two correctly: bias from a data source is a flaw in the data itself, in how it was collected or selected, whereas audience bias is a flaw in how the viewer interprets the visualisation, with an example for at least one
1 mark: Describes one type of bias correctly, or describes both as 'unfair' or 'wrong' without locating the bias in the data or in the viewer

sampleAnswers.answer: Bias from a data source is a flaw in the data itself, such as an online-only poll missing some residents, which undermines accuracy. Audience bias is a flaw in how viewers interpret a data visualisation, such as confirmation bias.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each bias is located correctly: the data source bias sits in the data, and the audience bias sits in interpretation, with an example of each. Both marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bias from a data source means the chart is biased. Audience bias means people can be biased when they look at the chart.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both biases are named but not located: the answer does not say whether the bias is in the data or in the viewer's interpretation, and gives no example. Say where each bias sits and give one example of each to earn two marks.

prompts.question: A tech company creates a data visualisation to show that its hiring process is fair. However, the data was collected via an opt-in survey sent only to current employees. Evaluate how unconscious bias and bias in the data source could lead to an inaccurate and misleading visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a technology company wants to publish a chart showing that its hiring process is fair. The chart uses responses from an opt-in survey sent only to current employees, and the analysts who designed it already expect a favourable result.
markerNotes: Evaluate means reach a judgement: here, whether the visualisation is misleading and how far the biases undermine the claim that hiring is fair.
Address both biases and how they interact: a skewed sample (data source bias) can be made to look favourable by analysts who choose metrics that match their expectations (unconscious bias).
Use the scenario's details: the opt-in design, the current-employee sample and the rejected applicants who are excluded.
commonStudentErrors: Describing unconscious bias in general without linking it to how the analysts would select or present the data in this case.
Listing both biases without evaluating how they combine to make the visualisation misleading.
Making an unsupported moral judgement that the company is 'lying' or 'unethical', rather than explaining how the visualisation becomes inaccurate.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates with sustained judgement how both biases compromise the visualisation, since the opt-in survey sent only to current employees excludes rejected applicants and favours satisfied respondents, while unconscious bias shapes which metrics are shown, and reaches a reasoned judgement on whether the chart can support the fairness claim
5 marks: Evaluates both sources of bias with specific links to the scenario and a judgement, but the evaluation of one bias or the judgement is less fully developed
4 marks: Explains both biases and how each could distort the visualisation, with links to the scenario, but without a clear evaluation of how serious the distortion is
3 marks: Explains one bias in relation to the scenario, or both biases with limited development, showing how the visualisation could mislead
2 marks: Identifies relevant biases, such as selection bias and unconscious bias, with little explanation of how they affect the visualisation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that bias can make a visualisation misleading, with no link to the scenario

sampleAnswers.answer:
The data source is fundamentally biased. Because the opt-in survey was sent only to current employees, it excludes the perspectives of applicants who were rejected, which is a severe form of selection bias: the people who may have experienced unfairness are not represented at all. The opt-in survey design adds a second distortion, since employees who are content with the process are more likely to respond, so the sample is skewed towards positive views before any analysis begins.

Unconscious bias compounds this. Analysts who expect the process to be fair may not intend to mislead, but they can choose metrics that look favourable, such as diversity figures for one department, while leaving out less flattering measures such as the ratio of applicants to hires for each demographic group. Each choice seems reasonable in isolation, yet together they shape what the audience sees and reduce the accuracy of the chart.

Ultimately, this misleading visualisation presents a precise-looking picture of fairness built on an unrepresentative dataset and a selective set of metrics. Its accuracy cannot support the claim that the hiring process is fair, and publishing it would damage the company's credibility once the gaps are discovered.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: both biases are evaluated with specific links to the scenario, and the opt-in survey and selection bias are shown to combine with unconscious bias. The conclusion is a reasoned judgement that the misleading visualisation cannot support the fairness claim.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bias in the data source is a problem here, because the survey was only sent to current employees. This means people who applied and were rejected are not included, so the results may not show what really happened in hiring. The survey was also opt-in, so people who were happy with the process may be more likely to answer. Analysts might also be unconsciously biased and choose to show the results that look good, which could make the chart misleading.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both biases are explained and linked to the scenario, which earns four marks. The answer describes how each could distort the chart but does not weigh how serious the distortion is or how the two combine to undermine the fairness claim. Add a judgement on how far the chart can be trusted to reach five marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The survey was only sent to current employees, so it is biased. Unconscious bias could also affect the analysts who make the chart, so the chart might not be accurate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two relevant biases are identified with little explanation, which earns two marks. Explain how the excluded applicants or the opt-in responses would skew the figures, and how the analysts' choices would show up in the chart.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate the effectiveness of software tools used to develop data visualisations (spreadsheets used to develop dashboards; presentation software used to present data analysis; business analytics services, including ‘as a service’ products; custom software solutions)

prompts.question: Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of using a spreadsheet to develop a data visualisation dashboard.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a small bakery owner wants a simple sales dashboard built from the sales records already kept in a spreadsheet. The owner has no budget for specialist software.
markerNotes: Give one of each: an advantage and a disadvantage. Two advantages, or two disadvantages, earn one mark.
Relate each point to dashboards: low cost matters for a small business, and limited interactivity matters when users want to filter the view.
A brief statement with a reason is enough; this is an identify question, not an evaluation.
commonStudentErrors: Giving two advantages, or two disadvantages, when the question asks for one of each.
Naming a spreadsheet feature, such as formulas, without saying whether it helps or hinders a dashboard.
Writing a vague point such as 'spreadsheets are good' or 'spreadsheets are hard' without a reason.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies one correct advantage of a spreadsheet for building a dashboard, such as low cost, familiarity or ease of setting up simple charts, and one correct disadvantage, such as limited interactivity or slow performance with large datasets, each clearly stated
1 mark: Identifies only one correct point, or gives two points of the same kind, both advantages or both disadvantages

sampleAnswers.answer: Spreadsheet software is an advantage for a data visualisation dashboard because it is low-cost and familiar to a small business owner. Its disadvantage is limited interactivity, and performance slows noticeably with large datasets.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One advantage and one disadvantage are identified, each with a reason tied to the owner's dashboard, so both marks are earned. The disadvantage correctly names interactivity and large datasets as the real limits of spreadsheets.

sampleAnswers.answer: An advantage of using spreadsheet software for data visualisation dashboards is its widespread availability and familiarity, making it an accessible and low-cost tool for basic data analysis.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The advantage is correct and clearly linked to the owner's situation, which earns one mark. The answer gives no disadvantage, so the second point is missing. Add a limitation such as weak interactivity or poor performance with large datasets.

prompts.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of using a business analytics service (e.g., Power BI, Tableau) compared to a custom software solution for a large enterprise's data visualisation needs.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a large bank must give its financial analysts secure, complex visualisations of trading and risk data. It is choosing between subscribing to a business analytics service, such as Power BI or Tableau, and commissioning a custom software solution built for its own systems.
markerNotes: Evaluate needs a judgement: weigh the trade-offs for a bank with secure, specialised needs and say which option is more effective and why.
Use the bank's requirements, such as security, complexity and specialised visualisations, as the criteria, and test each option against them.
Name concrete characteristics: rapid deployment and out-of-the-box dashboards for the service; integration and control over security for the custom solution.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Power BI or Tableau features without comparing them with custom software.
Assuming a custom solution is always better, without considering its higher cost, development time or maintenance.
Giving a judgement that is not connected to the bank's requirements, such as 'custom software is better' with no reason.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Evaluates both options against the bank's needs, weighing the speed, cost and feature range of the analytics service against the tailoring, security control and integration of the custom solution, and reaches a reasoned, scenario-specific judgement on which is more effective
4 marks: Evaluates both options with clear strengths and limitations linked to the bank's needs, with a judgement that is supported but not fully developed
3 marks: Explains the strengths and limitations of both options in relation to the scenario, without a direct comparison on a shared criterion or a judgement
2 marks: Describes one option's strengths or limitations with some relevance to the bank, without comparing it with the other
1 mark: Makes a general statement about analytics services or custom software, with no link to the bank's needs

sampleAnswers.answer:
Business analytics services such as Power BI or Tableau are highly effective for rapid deployment. Their out-of-the-box dashboards let the bank build and share visualisations quickly at a lower upfront cost. However, they offer limited customisation and may not meet every stringent data security protocol the bank requires.

Custom software solutions are less effective on speed and initial cost, because they need significant investment in development time and resources. Their primary strength is customisation: the visualisations can be integrated with proprietary trading and risk systems, can enforce the bank's own data governance rules, and can provide data security controls that an off-the-shelf product cannot.

For a large bank with complex and specific requirements, the custom solution is more effective overall, despite its higher cost, because it gives analysts a secure and precisely aligned tool. Its effectiveness rests on that fit rather than on speed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both options are evaluated against the bank's needs: the service is fast and cheaper but limited in customisation and data security, while the custom solution is slower and costlier but fits the bank's requirements. The reasoned judgement that it is more effective for this bank is supported by those criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: A business analytics service like Power BI is quick to set up and has many features, so it would suit the bank. However, it might not do everything the bank wants. A custom software solution would be more expensive, but it could be designed for the bank's needs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Strengths and limitations of both options are explained in relation to the bank, which earns three marks. The answer does not compare the options on a shared criterion such as security, or reach a judgement on which is more effective. Compare the two directly on security and specialisation, then conclude.

sampleAnswers.answer: Custom software is made just for one company, so it is special. Power BI is a program that people can subscribe to.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general statement about each option, with no evaluation of effectiveness and no link to the bank's needs, so one mark. Evaluate by stating a criterion, such as security control or speed of deployment, and judging how each option performs against it for the bank.

dotPoints.description: Interrogate data from a data visualisation (interpreting what you see; aggregation; filtering; the effect of outliers; reasoning)

prompts.question: Distinguish between aggregation and filtering in a data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional sales manager is using an interactive dashboard that shows monthly sales for every store in the company. She wants the total for each region, and then wants to look only at one product line.
markerNotes: Define each by its effect: aggregation reduces many values to one summary, while filtering shows fewer records but keeps each value as recorded.
A concrete example from the dashboard, such as total sales for a region against sales for one product line, makes the difference clear.
commonStudentErrors: Saying filtering and aggregation both 'summarise the data', without showing that filtering keeps the individual records.
Describing aggregation as 'removing data', which describes filtering.
Defining filtering as sorting the data into order.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Distinguishes the two correctly: aggregation combines many data points into a summary value, such as a total or average, while filtering selects a subset of records to display and leaves each value unchanged, with an example for at least one
1 mark: Defines one of the two correctly, or describes both as 'changing the data' without showing how they differ

sampleAnswers.answer: Aggregation combines many values into one summary, such as a regional total. Filtering selects a subset of records, leaving each value unchanged. Both let users interrogate data in an interactive dashboard, a form of data visualisation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each term is defined by its effect: aggregation combines many values into one summary, and filtering selects a subset of records while leaving each value unchanged. Both marks are earned, with a regional total as the example.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aggregation is when you add up sales data to get totals. Filtering is when you use the dashboard to look at the data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Aggregation is defined correctly, which earns one mark. Filtering is described only as 'looking at the data', which does not say that the dashboard selects a subset of records. Explain that filtering hides records that do not meet a condition, such as a product line, while leaving the values unchanged.

prompts.question: A bar chart shows the average monthly rainfall. One month is an extreme outlier, with a value five times higher than any other. Explain the effect of this outlier on the visualisation and the reasoning process of the viewer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a viewer is looking at a bar chart of average monthly rainfall for a coastal region, to understand its typical climate before planning a holiday. One month's bar is far taller than the rest because of an exceptional storm, and the viewer has not yet noticed it.
markerNotes: Answer both parts: the visual effect on the chart (the scale and the compressed bars) and the effect on the viewer's reasoning (a misleading conclusion about typical rainfall).
Set out the reasoning steps: noticing the tallest bar, assuming it is typical, then checking whether it is an exceptional event such as a storm.
A strong answer suggests what would help, such as a note on the chart, a median, or excluding the month.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the outlier 'wrong data' or 'a mistake' without evidence; the question is about its effect on the visualisation.
Explaining only the visual effect, without describing how the viewer's conclusion would change.
Claiming the outlier changes the values of the other months' bars, when it affects only its own month's bar and the scale.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains both effects precisely: the outlier stretches the axis scale, compressing the other bars so differences between months are hard to see, and it can mislead the viewer's reasoning into concluding the region is generally very wet. Shows how the viewer should interrogate the chart, such as by checking the axis scale or excluding the month, to reach a sound view of the typical climate
3 marks: Explains the outlier's effect on the scale and on the readability of the other bars, with a reasoned account of how this could mislead the viewer, but the reasoning process is described in less depth
2 marks: States that the outlier makes the scale or the other bars harder to read, or that the viewer might misunderstand the climate, without explaining the link between the two
1 mark: Makes a general statement that outliers are unusual or can affect charts, with no reference to this chart or to the viewer's reasoning

sampleAnswers.answer: The extreme outlier distorts the scale of the bar chart. The bar for that month is so tall that the axis stretches to accommodate it, flattening the other bars and making subtle differences between months hard to see. This affects the viewer's reasoning. A superficial look might lead to the incorrect conclusion that the region is extremely wet. Interpreting data carefully requires the viewer to reason that the spike is an exceptional storm, not a typical value, and to check the axis or mentally set the month aside, or use filtering tools to exclude it, before judging the typical rainfall.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both effects are explained: the stretched scale flattens the other bars, and the viewer could conclude the region is very wet unless they reason that the outlier is exceptional. The answer sets out the viewer's reasoning steps, which the question asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer: The outlier makes the bar chart's scale much bigger, so the other bars look small. This could make the viewer think the region has high rainfall all year round.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The visual effect and a possible misreading are both stated, which earns two marks. They are not explained as linked: the answer does not show how the squashed bars hide the typical months. Explain that step and the viewer's reasoning to reach three marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Outliers are unusual values in a dataset, and they can make charts look strange. Viewers should be careful when they read charts with outliers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a correct general statement about outliers, but it is not tied to this chart, so one mark. Refer to the bar chart, the scale and the rainfall month, and explain how the viewer would reason about the typical climate.

dotPoints.description: Use graphic design tools to assist in the graphic development of a data visualisation
Explain how user experience (UX) influences the development of effective data visualisations (relevance to the audience; audience interpretation; customisation; live analysis)

prompts.question: Explain why a data visualisation must be relevant to its intended audience.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a company is designing one dashboard of sales data for two users: its chief executive, who needs a quick view of company performance, and a data scientist who needs detailed data to test a forecasting model.
markerNotes: Explain the consequence of irrelevance: a summary that suits a CEO is useless to a data scientist, and detail that suits the data scientist overwhelms the CEO.
Refer to needs, goals and expertise as the reasons the audience matters.
A relevant example from the dashboard scenario makes the explanation specific.
commonStudentErrors: Saying relevance matters because it looks professional, rather than because it meets the audience's needs.
Writing that the audience must understand the chart, without explaining why different audiences need different detail.
Describing the CEO and the data scientist without relating their needs to the visualisation's design.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Explains why relevance matters: different audiences have different information needs, goals and levels of technical expertise, so a visualisation must show the detail and summary its audience can use to make decisions, with a relevant example of a mismatch
1 mark: States that a visualisation should be relevant or suited to its audience, without explaining why the audience's needs differ or what happens if they are not met

sampleAnswers.answer: Relevance matters because a data visualisation must suit its audience, whose expertise and needs differ. A CEO needs a summary dashboard, while a data scientist needs detail, so one design harms the user experience for one of them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer explains that audiences differ in expertise and needs, and gives the CEO and data scientist as an example of how one design fails one of them. Both marks are earned.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data visualisation should be relevant to its audience because it is important for people to get what they need from it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer states that relevance matters but does not say why audiences differ or what fails when a visualisation is not relevant to them. Explain that different users need different levels of detail and summary, and give an example of the mismatch.

prompts.question: Explain how incorporating 'customisation' and 'live analysis' features can improve the user experience of a data visualisation dashboard.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a company is developing an interactive sales dashboard for its field team, who work across several regions and check results on laptops and phones. Team members need current figures, and each focuses on the metrics for their own territory.
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism for each feature: customisation lets users remove what is irrelevant to them, and live analysis lets them act on current data rather than an outdated report.
Name the UX gain: less time searching, more relevant information and faster decisions.
Refer to the team's context, such as territories, laptops and phones, and time-sensitive decisions, to show why the features matter for these users.
commonStudentErrors: Defining customisation as 'changing the colours', which is cosmetic rather than a change to what the user sees.
Describing live analysis as 'modern' or 'the data is shiny' without saying what it lets the user do.
Writing about the two features separately, with no comment on how they work together for the team.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how customisation (such as personalised metrics, filters and layouts) and live analysis (data that updates as new records arrive, with interactive exploration) each improve UX through efficiency, relevance and better decision-making, with a specific example for the sales team and a clear account of why the two work together
3 marks: Explains how both features improve UX with a relevant link to the sales team, but one feature is developed in less depth or the link between the features and UX is not clearly explained
2 marks: Describes one feature in some detail and its UX benefit, or both features in general terms, without showing how each improves the experience
1 mark: Makes a general statement that customisation or live data is good, with no explanation of how it improves UX

sampleAnswers.answer: Customisation improves the user experience of an interactive dashboard by giving each user control. A salesperson can filter the view to the metrics for their own territory, removing noise, so the dashboard is more efficient to use. Live analysis adds real-time data, so the team can act on current figures rather than a report that is already outdated. This supports faster decision-making in the field, where staff on phones and laptops need immediate answers. Together, the two features keep the dashboard's relevance high at the moment of use, so each user gets a better experience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both features are explained by their effect on the user experience: customisation removes irrelevant information, and live analysis supports immediate decisions. Each is linked to the field team's needs, and the closing point explains why the two work together, which earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Customisation lets a salesperson change the dashboard so it shows what they need, which makes it easier to use. Live data is also useful because it updates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both features are named with a general benefit, which earns two marks. The answer does not explain how each feature improves the experience, such as by reducing the information a user must search through, or by allowing decisions on current figures. Expand each point with its effect on the user.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dashboards with customisation and live analysis are better. People like modern things and they are more fun to use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This is a general claim that the features are good, with no explanation of how they improve UX, so one mark. Explain what customisation lets the salesperson do and how live data changes the decisions the team can make.

dotPoints.description: Develop and implement criteria for evaluating the effectiveness of user experiences

prompts.question: Identify two criteria that could be used to evaluate the user experience (UX) of a data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a design team has built a new dashboard for a hospital's ward managers and wants to check that it works for them before launch. The team needs criteria it can measure in a usability test.
markerNotes: A criterion must be measurable: name what is evaluated, such as clarity of understanding or time to find information, rather than a general quality such as 'good'.
Two different criteria are needed; 'easy to use' and 'user friendly' are the same criterion.
Briefly say what each criterion measures for the audience, which makes it usable in an evaluation.
commonStudentErrors: Giving visual features such as colour or font as criteria, rather than qualities of the user's experience.
Naming two wordings of one criterion, such as 'easy to use' and 'user friendly'.
Using a vague criterion such as 'it looks good', which cannot be evaluated.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct, relevant UX criteria for a data visualisation, such as clarity (how easily the audience understands the information), efficiency (how quickly users find what they need) or audience interpretation, each named clearly
1 mark: Identifies one relevant criterion, or names two criteria that are really the same, such as 'easy to use' and 'user friendly'
